utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we'll take one adjournment, at about 12.00, for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: General Maisonneuve, would you tell the Court your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Joseph Omer Michel Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And General Maisonneuve, I understand that you are currently a Major General. You are presently the Assistant Deputy Chief of the Defence Staff for the Canadian Armed Forces in Ottawa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is it also fair to say, sir, that you've spent about 30 years in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You've been an armoured officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, sir, have you been involved in the command of troops?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. I have commanded troops all the way up to unit command, which is a regimental command, and also have served time as a staff officer in major operations and in formations in Canada and abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just before we move on to that, a unit, just for people like me who --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: About a thousand -- a thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And, sir, when you said you've also served abroad, have you spent any time in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I spent one year as the Chief of Operations for UNPROFOR, from 1993 to 1994. That's my time in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And do you have any experience in training troops in all-arms combat?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have trained troops, and I have trained with troops up to a brigade level, which is a formation of about 5.000 people, participation in many exercises and manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And in addition to being in the Balkans, do you have any other experience abroad?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I have spent three tours in Cyprus with the UN mission there. I've also spent two years in France and on exchanges with the US army, US armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you become involved with KVM, the Kosovo Verification Mission, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In November of 1998, I was sent to Vienna to head the KVM support unit for about three weeks, and then I was asked to deploy to Kosovo to head the first Regional Centre to be opened in Prizren. I spent essentially three months there, until the mission was evacuated in March of 1999, and I then went into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. We'll get back to your involvement there later on. Now, sir, did you in fact provide a statement to the officials of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 10th of March in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity of reviewing that statement, making some minor corrections as recently as yesterday, the 28th of May, 2002?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at that time, sir, did you solemnly declare that the contents of that statement with the attachments and with those amendments you pointed out were true to the best of your information, knowledge, and belief?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that statement at this point be entered as an exhibit in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 175.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, you have the benefit or will have the benefit shortly of copies of the 92 bis statement of this witness. Pursuant to the request of the Trial Chamber to take part of this witness's evidence live, the version of the statement that we are now distributing has in fact received numbering of paragraphs for ease of reference. So the advanced copy that the Court may have received in order to determine whether it was appropriate to bis him has now got paragraph numbers, and it might be of assistance to you to know that I propose to deal live with paragraphs 21 through 37, which deal with the VJ; paragraphs 42, and then 45 through 50 which deal with his connection with the MUP. And those are the paragraphs that I want to deal with live.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're also going to deal with Racak live.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And that is contained in those paragraphs that I've just outlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: General Maisonneuve, is it fair to say, sir, that in your statement, the way it was taken, the first seven paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps might the witness also have a copy of this before him to -- it would assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do have a copy, actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Paragraphs 1 through 7 deal with your background, is that correct, setting up of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And then paragraphs 8 through 20 deal with the OSCE/KVM mission that you've -- that are contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And then at paragraph 21, you -- from paragraphs 21 through to paragraph -- sorry, I think it's -- 37, you deal with the incidents at Racak and your observations of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And then moving to paragraph 38, you deal with the Ministry of the Interior, or the MUP, right through to paragraph 52.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thereafter, you speak about the KLA and the KVM Refugee Task Force in Albania, which starts at paragraph 56.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Turning, if I may, to those areas that I, at the Court's request, will be asking you some further detailed questions, you've already told us, sir, that you joined the KVM, I believe, in Vienna in -- I believe it was in 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: November of 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, at some point, did you become the head of the KVM's Regional Centre in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes I did. That would have in been the middle of December of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this Regional Centre, is that the RC Prizren? Is that what they're referred to in the documentation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's referred to in the documentation. What it was, the KVM itself covered all of Kosovo but it was divided into five Regional Centres, basically covering the five administrative districts of Kosovo, and Prizren was the administrative district in which my Regional Centre was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to leave a little bit of space between my next question to allow for translation. Sir, to your knowledge, were there any VJ brigades with elements positioned in the RC Prizren, which was your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. There were essentially two brigades operating in my Regional Centre. The 549th Brigade operated out of Prizren itself. That's where its headquarters was, with the main responsibilities of the border with Albania. And there was an element of the 243rd Brigade, which was based in Urosevac, which also had some elements deployed within the administrative district of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you've told us that there were five different Regional Centres. The area of Racak/Stimlje, was that wholly within your area of RC Prizren or was that on the border of -- with another RC district or what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It was actually totally within Regional Centre 5, which is the Pristina Regional Centre, but right outside my area, near the boundary between my area and Regional Centre 5, so it was in RC 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And returning to the two VJ brigades, the 549th and the 243rd, do you know whether they were part of a larger organisation within the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. Both of them belong to the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Well, if I might just distinguish between the two. Let's start with the 549. Do you know what type of a brigade that was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It was a motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Motorised brigade, which means it was carried in mostly trucks and dismounted a lighter brigade. Obviously for the reason that it was operating mainly along the border region, and so in very wooded operations, they could not use heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You say they operated mainly along the border. Was that because of -- was there a particular area of jurisdiction that they were involved in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. That was their area of responsibility, was taking care of the border. They had border battalions that belonged to them and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that brigade was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Colonel Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you ever meet Colonel Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how would you describe him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would describe him as a -- a professional soldier. He was actually quite straightforward and we always had very productive discussions when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you in fact -- you mentioned that you had discussions. Did you in fact have a meeting with Colonel Delic on the 4th of February of 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Colonel Delic, I believe, was the 1st of February. Yes, it was the 1st of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. I got you the wrong date. 1st of February, yes. And attached to your statement, sir, did you produce minutes that were recorded of your meeting with Colonel Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In fact, every meeting that I attended with members of the parties, I would always have a note-taker with me that would then produce a record of meeting. In this case, when I met him on the 1st of February, we had some discussions. Primarily I wished to open a field office near the border, and so we were in discussions of his responsibilities and whether this was within his authorities or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could ask you to turn, if you would, please, to the attachment that's -- it's got a number of numbers, but it's dated the 1st of February, 1999, and it's entitled "Record of discussions, visit to commander VJ Brigade Prizren, held at officers' recreation facility." Do Your Honours have that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, do you -- do you have that particular document in the bundle?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You have that as well. All right. Well, sir, these were the minutes that were taken by your assigned note-taker? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Captain Chris Weissflog.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And he is in the list of people that are noted to have attended that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And there is a legend of initials at the top of that document, showing "D" meaning Colonel Delic, "M" meaning you, and then the other participants are also listed on that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, what can you tell us of this -- first of all, you've reviewed this document, and does it accurately compare with your recollection of what went on at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, can you tell us, if you would, please, what significance you attach to these particular notes of the meeting that you had with Colonel Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, in essence, it shows that Colonel Delic did not have a completely free hand. He was not operating individually in his brigade area. He was part of a chain of command, as any military force that I, of course, have come in contact with usually does. He -- I was asking him to -- to agree to open a field office near Pleneja, which was within five kilometres of the border area, and he was explaining that he did not have the authorisation and he had to seek it from higher. I also got a sense, of course, that he was a disciplined officer and that his forces obeyed to his commands. I had previously dealt with him and received the same type of sense from him. If you go to the next page--

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just before we do that, if I may, on this document there are dots or bullet points. This reference that you make to the fact that he needed higher command, is that reflected --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Fifth bullet there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fifth bullet point. All right. And there's a "D" ascribed there.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's Delic speaking that he wasn't personally against Pleneja but he felt he must have authorisation from his command, i.e., from higher command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right. And you were about to address our attention to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. If you go to the next page, the second bullet down, where he says, "I'm not authorised to decide on this," and he talks about General Loncar, who was the liaison, VJ liaison officer at the Pristina level, and Delic says that he's not the commander, he's a liaison officer, and therefore he had no authority. Loncar had who no authority to agree to the deployment of the field office.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the reference to, "I am not authorised to decide on this," what was the reference to what he was not authorised to decide on? Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. This is the question of whether we would be allowed to patrol near the -- within the five-kilometre area of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And again, that was outside -- he said that was outside the scope of his authority?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Turning to the next page, three of four, about halfway down the page, we see the sixth bullet point down on the page, again there's the initial "D." What, if anything, do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, here he -- this is where I got a sense that he was firmly in control of his forces where I was telling him that his people had been intimidating the locals, and he -- he was saying there that intimidation by his forces, he saw that as a breach discipline and that he -- he always thought, or he always told me that he would deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So this -- from your meeting with Delic, then, you came to the opinions that you've earlier stated, and these are some of the --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- things that you point to in terms of why you arrived at those decisions. Okay. Well, if we could move very briefly, then, sir, time is of the essence to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do, do you want these exhibits entered?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. They are part of the bis package, so they are part of the last exhibit number, but it might be of some -- I'm in the Court's hands as to whether you think it would be assistance to the Court to have them with separate numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it would be of assistance since some of the package are documents which have already been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And not all of the documents that are attached to the bis package, so to speak, will be actually referred to. They're part of the bis'ing but they're not part of the live examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us, therefore, give these separate exhibit numbers now, and any additional documents that you want exhibited which were in the package, you can refer to later, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we give this a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 176.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I might then turn, if that meets with Your Honours' approval, to the 243rd Brigade. You mentioned there were two brigades. What type of brigade was it and who was its commander, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: This was a mechanised brigade, meaning it was -- soldiers there were carried in armoured personnel carriers, and its commander was Colonel Jelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And -- I'm sorry. You've told us earlier what a motorised brigade was. What is a mechanised brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's what I say, their soldiers were carried in armoured vehicles, armoured personnel carriers, and therefore they were equipped with armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My ignorance of military terms is obvious, I'm sorry. And do you know where they were based?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: They were based in Urosevac. This is where the headquarters of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And do you know which elements, if any, of that brigade fell within the RC Prizren's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. The -- the Urosevac brigade had a combat team, a force of about 150 people with tanks and armoured personnel carriers, deployed on the Dulje Heights. This was one of the agreed-to deployed combat teams. But also outside of their barracks, they had other elements which -- they had basically a company of all-arms deployed also in the area of Racak on top of the -- as well as the combat team in Dulje. So they had a couple of elements outside their barracks. The Dulje combat team was within my area of responsibility and, therefore, I had to have relations with the brigade headquarters in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Now, you may have answered this in the course of your question [sic], but was Racak then within the 243rd's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you hear of an incident in early January involving the KLA near Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: A couple of -- a couple of incidents we heard about, one of which happened directly within my area of responsibility. On the 8th of January - so about a week before Racak - there had been an ambush carried out by the KLA in Stimlje pass, which was a very narrow pass that went through the Dulje Heights. And my -- my people arrived on the scene right after the ambush. There had been -- two policemen were killed right at the moment of the ambush and then another policeman, MUP policeman died in the hospital later, and we took the KLA to task on that one. And there was also another incident involving -- and that one was outside my area of responsibility, was within RC5's area of responsibility, involving again the MUP and a police car that I understood had burned or something like that. This was an incident that happened much closer to the time of Racak. So there had been a couple of incidents by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You said you took the KLA to task on that. Was there a particular individual you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. My main contact for the entire Prizren Regional Centre was a KLA commander who called himself Drini. So I met with him right after the ambush to explain to him that this was not -- these were -- this was firmly against the agreement, against the ceasefire, that he was only inviting retaliation by doing these -- doing these things. And at that point, he commented that he had not personally ordered the ambush, it had been accomplished by a -- one of his local commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Well, moving then to the Racak incident itself, the 15th of January. Did you at some point become aware of an operation by Serb forces near Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th of January, the -- General DZ had -- who is the Deputy Head of Mission for operations, had called a meeting of all Regional Centre heads in Pec. At about -- well, towards -- throughout the morning, we'd been receiving reports of an operation against Racak by the VJ and the MUP, and -- to the point where it seemed to be a very -- very important -- a major operation, and therefore, General DZ asked me to go down to -- to take over the operation. Because the operation was in Regional Centre 5, the commander of Regional Centre 5 had not yet been deployed, been appointed, and so he asked me -- General DZ asked me to go and take command of the operation even though it was outside of my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And did you or did KVM have verifiers near Racak at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had a couple of patrols from Regional Centre 5 and, of course, when I was tasked to go down there, I actually dispatched a couple of my own patrols as well to go to Racak and assist Regional Centre 5's patrols on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do you know, generally speaking, what sort of vantage point they would have had? Were they --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. Our patrols actually were on the heights surrounding Racak and observing the operation. They observed VJ tanks firing into houses that we believe were occupied because we could see plumes of smoke. And in fact, in those houses, we went down after the firing stopped and let the people out of the basements. These are the reports that I received from my -- my verifiers. I myself arrived on the ground at about 4.30 in the afternoon, and as I was proceeding towards there, I was receiving reports of the firing and so on, which stopped about 3.30. The forces from the VJ and the MUP pulled back at that point, and so when I was travelling towards the -- towards Racak, the -- the day was coming to a -- it was January, so -- so darkness fell very quickly, and so instead of going into the village of Racak, I was told they were -- that my people had actually picked up some Albanian wounded and were going to bring them to -- to the hospital. So I decided to go to the hospital and to get the hospital ready to receive the wounded. The hospital was situated right beside the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I can just back up a little bit. You've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. indicated that you had your verifiers up in the hills. I believe you indicated that they observed VJ tanks firing into houses. When you say "VJ tanks," are we talking --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: T55s were the type of tanks that they were using. So there were T55s. There were also -- I had some of my people in -- observing the area around and in particular that area that I was mentioning where they had -- the VJ had also deployed an element and saw some of the howitzers pointed towards Racak and the villages surrounded -- surrounding the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did they report seeing any similar type of weaponry in the village itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No tanks in the village, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did the MUP have tanks and heavy equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: MUP did not have tanks. They had -- but they had Pragas and armoured vehicles, VRDMs and so on. They didn't have tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So if there was a T55 tank, that would have been VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That was a VJ, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did they report seeing the MUP at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, the MUP were in the village. My assessment after receiving all the reports, and I put the assessment in -- in my statements, my assessment was that the VJ had provided long-range support, if you wish, around the village, support to the operation that was carried out by the -- by the MUP. The house-to-house search and the cleaning of the village, if you wish, was done by the MUP, dismounted MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. General Maisonneuve, because of your extensive experience, do you have any personal experience with the use of tanks or heavy artillery and other heavy weaponry in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, in exercises and manoeuvres certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Have you ever trained in or planned anti-insurgency operations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I have not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, in fact, heavy weapons -- I'm an armoured officer and so use of tanks and use of armoured infantry is usually done for -- it's not used in counter-insurgency operations. It's usually done for major combat engagements in wide open spaces and against armoured enemy. If you're going to use -- anti-insurgency operations are usually done by much lighter forces than tanks and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are there any reports that the KLA had tanks and heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, the KLA do not have tanks. Certainly not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, from your experience, would it ever be appropriate for tanks or anti-aircraft weapons or artillery or weaponry of the kind to fire at civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. In fact, this was one of the points I made to the brigade commander from Urosevac when I did meet him, was that I thought that the use of such weapons in firing against civilian targets such as houses when in fact we had not observed any fire being returned or in fact any fire previous to the tanks firing into the houses was indiscriminate and inappropriate use of force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, what would be the more appropriate way of dealing with that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if there is no -- if there's no firing coming from a house, then you would deploy infantry and move up to the house. If you're fired upon, obviously you would return fire, but professional force does not fire unless -- unless there's a need to fire. If there is a need to bring supporting fire down, you would do it with small arms and so forth. So you actually deal with -- with an enemy with usually proportional forces. There's no doubt that if you need to, you would amass vastly superior forces so that you're prepared to deal with anything but if you're not being fired at, you would not indiscriminately fire and certainly not with heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir -- I'll just wait for translation. Were you or your observers aware of a KLA presence in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: We were aware of -- of light KLA presence, and in fact, it was confirmed by the -- certainly in statements by the KLA to me after, that the village had been lightly not even defended, if you wish, but they had scouts and a few fighters in the village. But this was not a place that we considered was held by a very strong KLA force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us about this particular incident in Racak and the observation of tanks and heavy artillery. During the remainder of your stay in Kosovo, were there other times where you saw Serb forces direct heavy weapons against civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Oh, that happened on several occasions. It seemed to be the modus operandi of the Serb security forces that any type of provocation, no matter how small, would result in an overwhelming use of force disproportionate to the actions of the KLA or the perpetrators, and this was constantly one of the things that I reinforced to the Serbs but also to the KLA when I met with them, saying I don't know why you're provoking them because you know that it always results in disproportionate use of force. For example, in the Stimlje pass where I said the three policemen eventually died there that were ambushed by the KLA, within -- within a few minutes, a tank pulled out of the Dulje combat team position and moved out so it could fire directly into a village called, I believe, Slapuzane. A small village, firing into the village without any provocation, firing at civilian houses and would automatically cause -- you know, any time this would happen, it would automatically cause the locals to pick up whatever they had on their -- you know, and move out of the village, stream out of the village to the next village until things quieted down and then they'd come back. But it was -- you know, this type of retaliation always happened, always seemed to me to be, certainly in my opinion, disproportionate and overwhelming and actually just indiscriminate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Sir, returning to the 15th of January for a moment. I think you've told us already that you went to the hospital to prepare them to receive wounded as a result of the things that you had seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Did you see the police that evening? When I say police, I mean the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, yes. I saw a couple of MUP soldiers or members of the MUP that came over to the hospital, and they were arrogant and were wondering why we were trying to get the doctor up and were not at all pleased to see us roust the doctor and the ambulance to provide help to the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. The following day, the 16th of January, sir, what if anything did you do that day that's relevant to the proceedings before the court?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, on the 15th in the evening, I organised for my patrols to return early in the morning. I also wanted a presence by Regional Centre 5 patrols in the village, and so we decided that we were going to go back and come back early the next morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, you're being asked, if you would, to slow down for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. So the 16th in the morning, my verifiers arrived approximately 7.00 in the morning in Racak, and reports started filtering back from them that they had -- they were finding bodies and that a major operation had actually taken place the night before in Racak. By the time I made my way to Racak, it was approximately 9.00 in the morning. I went in and observed -- I went in Racak myself and observed the -- a few bodies, and I had -- and they were bodies of elderly -- elderly men. And I had then also prepared a meeting with the brigade commander from Urosevac who I thought was going to show up on the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Before we get to that meeting, if I may, sir, some of your observations. Did you attend an area known as the gully?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And this would have been -- but this would have been after my meeting, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I'll come back to that. We'll go to the meeting -- we'll try to deal with the 16th in a chronological fashion, then. You tried to arrange a meeting with whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: With Colonel Jelic, the brigade commander from Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That would be the 243rd.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The 243rd. And he did not show up but his liaison officer did, a Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. And again, did you have a note-taker with you for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I did. And I believe the notes are attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can ask you to turn to the attachment, it appears to be a two-page attachment, dated the 16th of January, RC Prizren, "Record of discussions visit to 243 Brigade Urosevac, held at Brigade Headquarters at Urosevac" and with four people attending, in the legend

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 15, at the bottom of the page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, according to the legend, sir -- again, this is a formality: This is an accurate record and accords with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What can you tell us, sir, about this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, this was a meeting where -- where, of course, I was incensed after -- after seeing the damage and the dead bodies, and I was actually coming to take the brigade commander to task and ask him to confirm that he had been involved, that his forces had been involved. I also mentioned the Tribunal. And at that point, Lieutenant Colonel Petrovic confirmed that the MUP had actually participated, had actually done the action, but had been supported by a Praga and a tank from the brigade, from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And your allegations and his response are reflected in these notes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The third -- the third bullet point is "M," that's you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You said you saw atrocities in Racak, you assessed VJ and MUP were responsible?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: "Fifty people killed, non-combatants." Did you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what else did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned all the -- you know, the fact that his tanks and heavy artillery had moved out and that the -- they still had not moved back to their barracks, which was against the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: And then I -- of course, I was speaking with the liaison officer, this was not the brigade commander. So I was not happy not to be able to speak to the brigade commander himself to mention that to him. And then at the end when I -- or at the beginning -- at the end of my state -- first statement when I mentioned, "Do you have anything to say?" and you see I think it's bullet about eight down, where he says, "Stimlje was done by the MUP with Praga -- Praga armoured vehicles and one tank," and then I guess understood there that this was the VJ in support.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right. So basically he's blaming it on the MUP with support from the VJ at that point?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. And then I -- that's the -- the next bullet is where I mention the Tribunal and the fact that I thought that this behaviour was certainly not in keeping with a professional army's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you then have a second meeting with VJ officers at a later date?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to exhibit that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 177.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: On the 16th, I also met with the MUP commander in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Before we move to the MUP commander in Stimlje -- I'll return to that, if I may, later. I want to go from your meeting with Petrovic, who was the liaison officer for the VJ, to a subsequent meeting you had on the 4th of February, still with the VJ --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- and compare and/or contrast what occurred or what you were told at that second meeting.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. The second meeting, I'd been -- right from the 16th of January, I had been attempting to meet with the commander of the brigade from Urosevac and had on a number of occasions requested meetings, and it didn't happen until the 4th of January, and that's recorded in the record of discussion at page 18 at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the 4th of February 1999 "Record of discussions visit to commander of VJ Brigade Urosevac" at the -- I think it's pages 18, 17, and 16 of the attachments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, sir, again attending - we have a legend - again you have your note-taker taking these notes, and again, this accords with your recollection of what transpired?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And we have you there. We have, among other people, we have Colonel Kotur, the VJ chief liaison officer to the KVM headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And "D" is Colonel Krsman Jelic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. It actually should be a "J." In the legend, that should be a "J" throughout the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And Petrovic, the chap you spoke to earlier, was also present?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, what happened at that meeting and what if anything is of significance in your --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in this -- this meeting I was -- again I was unhappy because he had refused to meet me or certainly had not met me until I had almost forced him and through, I think it's through Colonel Kotur, that I was able to meet him. Again, I mentioned or I -- I asked him where he had been on the day, and he -- he was rather evasive about where he was. He also would not confirm that -- that he had operated with the MUP during the Racak operation. He was saying that in fact his forces had not fired into the village but had fired in the outskirts towards other -- another two villages, Belince and -- I can't remember the name of the other village. But the point was that he did not -- he did not confirm that his forces were actually operating along with the MUP at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did he acknowledge that VJ forces were in fact operational?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Oh, he did, and he -- their approach there was that the MUP and the VJ were operating independently but simultaneously, which was -- which is probably -- it's totally against -- it's just so farfetched because in any military operation, the one thing you want to do when you're firing real bullets is to make sure that you are coordinated down to the most exact manner; and the way you do this coordination and cooperation is you meet ahead of time to discuss areas where your forces will be operating, where you will base your forces. You discuss points of coordination such as reporting lines, areas where you're going to fire, direct your fire, means of coordination, such as radio call signs, you ensure that your frequencies are all the same so that you're all operating on the same radio nets. It's got to be -- I mean, if you're firing real bullets, you don't want to have blue-on-blue engagements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This is an obvious question, but why do you need that kind of coordination?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Because you don't want to have your friendly forces firing against friendly forces and you want to be able to -- you want to be able to direct your forces and command them properly. So in my -- in my military opinion, there had to be coordination between the MUP and the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: To what extent and to what level?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I would say certainly at the brigade level. This was an operation that involved, you know, significant forces from both the MUP and the VJ, and so I would say a brigade or higher level perhaps even.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did "J," which I guess is Jelic, acknowledge responsibility for that brigade? And I'm asking you to turn to page which is written -- it's number 17. And I think there are a bunch of bullet points that start with a question to you or by you of Jelic whether or not he was the officer in charge for the VJ forces on the ground at Racak on the 15th of January. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In fact, he responds that, "This is a brigade and I'm responsible for the whole region." He was in fact responsible for the whole brigade. There is no denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And does this page 17 there, it almost seems to be an attempt at a transcript of the narrative conversation that takes place. Is that -- to the best of your recollection, is that an accurate portrayal of how it went?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how the discussion went.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, as you're listening to this explanation, what was your impression? Were you buying it or did you accept it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I did not buy it. I thought he was very evasive in his -- in his explanations and seemed to be tap dancing around the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how did this explanation compare, in your opinion, with the explanation you'd received from Petrovic just days earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, it didn't jive. Certainly Petrovic, to my mind, had confirmed that tanks and Praga had been involved, tanks from the VJ had been involved, and luckily, I think in this case, I had managed to speak to Petrovic very quickly after the actual operation so that he had not had time to receive the party line, if you wish, from his brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just one more question about this area, sir. Did your observers report to you seeing VJ forces engaging targets between Racak and Belince on the 16th of January as Colonel Jelic attempted to explain to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What did they see instead?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: They said they saw -- they told me that they saw tanks shooting into houses that were on the outskirts of Racak that were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You were about to turn to your meeting of the 16th of January with the MUP when I asked you to turn to that. Could we do that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, is covered in paragraphs 45 to 50 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 4th of February exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 178.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now -- and I'm going to ask you, Your Honours, the document 16th of January, with the MUP, is pages 13, 12, and 11 of the attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Again, sir, this is a record of -- of a meeting that you held with Janicijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Correct, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And he was the chief of the MUP, was he?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: He was the chief of police in the area of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And very quickly, sir, could you tell us the significant aspects of the -- of this particular conversation and --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: There are a few interesting aspects. First of all, he described the operation from his point of view. I was looking for -- myself and Gil Gilbertson, who was the deputy head of RC 5 - in fact, he was the one asking most of the questions in this case - we were looking for who was in charge of the -- of the actual operation and who had commanded it and how many people had been involved. He confirmed that there were approximately 100 of his members involved. He also confirmed that he was in charge. I believe if you go to page 2, or to the second page of the statement, at the top, about five or six bullets down, he confirms that a hundred men were involved. And about two-thirds of the way down, I asked him if he was in charge of the 100 policemen, and he said, "If it is of your concern, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And during that conversation, was it put to him that the VJ basically blamed the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I about -- again about two-thirds of the way down, just a little below the 100 policemen statement, Gil in fact says that, "We just left the VJ; they put the blame on you." And he denies that they were with the VJ. And the MUP in fact maintain that this was a MUP operation without VJ involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what was your impression of this particular meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Again, this was another meeting where I thought that the answers did not match what actually happened on the ground, and they produced with great elan the weapons that they said they'd captured during the operation; a 50 calibre machine-gun and a grenade -- grenade launcher. But this did not match my view of what happened and what my observers had seen on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Dealing with paragraph 42 of your statement, how would you generally describe the MUP's behaviour towards the KVM and the Kosovo Albanian population, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, in all my dealings with the MUP, I believe they tried to -- I believe our relationships with the OSCE, KVM, and the MUP were -- relationship was professional, straightforward. My -- the chief of police in the Prizren area certainly tried to portray himself as a professional police officer who was well aware of community policing, community policing approach, and so that's how he liked to portray himself. But on the ground, I -- certainly we found another -- another approach. We found that at many of the checkpoints, the police were overbearing, arrogant, sometimes beat up innocent civilians. And their behaviour was usually only tempered when we had people immediately at the scene. So in some of the major checkpoints, I refused to let my people leave, and I would set up permanent observation posts because I knew that that was the way that the -- the only way that the police would actually behave according to normal -- what I thought were normal standards of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 179.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I invited you earlier to give us comments about things you actually saw at the gully, and you indicated that you'd had a meeting and I said we'd come back to it. Let's come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. After coming back to -- back to Racak, I was told that General DZ and Ambassador Walker were actually going to come to Racak, and so I went back into the village and my verifiers took me up to the area that you referred to as the gully. At that location were about 20 bodies from what I could count. They were laid in a bit of a line. It was one particular area where there were about eight or ten bodies together. From what I could see, they had been shot at close range, most in the head -- mostly in the head, the back or the front, and -- and the men were -- they were all men, first of all, and they all -- they did not look like men of what I would consider fighting age. They looked like several elderly people, mostly villagers, some wearing the typical Albanian caps there, and they looked like, as I say, they had been -- they would have been shot from -- from close range.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: From what you could see, was there any evidence to you, just as a professional person but as a layman, that these -- as to whether or not these bodies were shot in situ or are you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I could not tell that. The one thing I did -- I do remember, though, is the bodies, some of them were covered in dew, and dew comes down, of course, in the morning, so would have been there certainly in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, what time did you see these bodies in the gully?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say probably around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: A.M.?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: A.M., yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, had you, as part of the KVM, heard reports earlier about men and women being separated and men going missing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I'd heard that on, you know, different occasions. Certainly in the case of Racak, I saw a report after the -- after the -- the actual incident and probably a few days later that said that some -- some of the men had been rounded up. My verifiers didn't report that to me directly, but of course the KVM, at their level, had reports from all the Regional Centres, including Regional Centre 5, and I heard reports then that some 20 men had been separated from their wives and taken away at some point during the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at the time those reports were prepared, was that before or after these bodies were found in the gully, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I can't really say but I would say before they were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir - I'm trying to finish you in about an hour - so I have just a few more questions. I think you've answered most of this already, the degree of coordination of forces would be involved in an operation like Racak, and I think you've given us partially the answer that I was anticipating. The other aspect of it would be the firing by VJ or firing by an army unit. How do you avoid friendly fire casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, again as I mentioned, the only way to avoid that is to coordinate ahead of time -- ahead of the operation that -- that portions and elements will fire in a certain area and other elements will fire in another area, and you do that by -- on a map, say, drawing a line or drawing a coordination measure that allows you to say, okay, move your fire from here to there at this time or on my order. And as your other friendly forces progress, the fire gets moved over, if you wish. And that way -- this is the type of coordination that has to take place before an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My final question, then, sir, is: What -- if you were asked to sum up, what was your assessment of the military operation in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, my -- my assessment is that it was -- it would be an operation that -- that was against very lightly-defended -- a lightly-defended locality that used as -- as was the modus operandi heavy, indiscriminate firing in overwhelming fire against civilians and -- and certainly the bodies found throughout the village, which in fact when I -- after DZ and Ambassador Walker left, I went back and personally saw one young lady, probably 18 years old, and a 12-year-old boy among the bodies, and so I would say that this was not a legitimate -- legitimate military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you finish, we have attached to the statement - it may be as well if you get the witness just to briefly go through them - various reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have in mind the -- yes. The report of the 17th of January, I think it is, or 15th and 16th of January, pages 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wrote that myself, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It would be helpful just if the witness would go through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If you have a copy of that --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- there, perhaps you could just very briefly assist Their Honours with respect to your notations there.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. In fact, Your Honour, that kind of resumes the points I've been making throughout that in fact on the 15th I was at a meeting and I was sent to the area of Racak to look after the operation. I went to the hospital, and we evacuated some casualties, and I decided at that point that we should -- on the 15th, that we should meet with the commander of the brigade in Urosevac to discuss these actions. It speaks then on the 16th of January about our patrols going into -- into Racak, my arrival and briefing, then the meeting at the officers' club in Urosevac with the -- in fact, at that time it was not the brigade commander, it was with Petrovic, the liaison officer. Then the MUP chief. And when it says, "report attached," those are two reports that you've already, I believe, admitted as exhibits. Then I briefed the Deputy Head of Mission Operations and the Head of Mission, and -- and that essentially recounts the rest of the day. And at the end is my assessment, as I mentioned, I believe, earlier, of the events as I saw them. That's the evening of the 16th. When I came back, I wrote this report, that I -- my assessment was that the VJ had provided long -- long-range fire support from the high ground surrounding Racak while the MUP did the house-to house clearing and the dismounted operations within -- within Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That should be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 180.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If you could turn next, if you would, to your report on page 8. I believe Their Honours expressed an interest in that. Just wait for a moment, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I've asked the witness also to look at your page 8, because I believe that's the other area of interest to the Court that you've expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just before you do that, I just wanted to ask the general on what did he base the assessment that the VJ provided long-range support?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's based on my discussions with my verifiers on the ground who had been actually -- and I actually also went up to, you know -- throughout the day that I was touring around the village of Racak, I actually went up to the high ground above Racak where my verifiers had seen the tanks providing support. And of course, I make that assessment from -- based on their reports and reports of all the other verifiers in the area and my own military assessment of how I would carry out such an operation. If it had been a heavily-defended locality, that's how I would have carried out the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you then very briefly, Major General, turn to page 8, which is the report of activities of the RC 1 Prizren for the 17th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. This -- obviously I wrote this one on the evening of the 17th after the operations of the day, and we were -- we were advised at this point that on the morning of the -- on the -- on the morning of the 17th, that the Yugoslav authorities wished to -- to have a -- perform an investigation, and that they wanted to do so with -- with a large element of security provided by the MUP. So I met with the Deputy Head of Mission, General DZ, in Stimlje before 8.00, and we agreed that I would then take three patrols into the city -- into the village, sorry, of Racak and its surroundings to -- to keep an eye on what was going on actually in the village. There was a KLA presence in the village at that point, and I coordinated the movements of my patrols while General DZ was meeting with the presiding judge. Around 11.00, she had refused to actually go into the village escorted by the KVM and still wanted to go in with a heavy MUP force, and in fact, they began their movement shortly thereafter, and I had to evacuate the OSCE patrols who were very close to the firing that was ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: A couple of questions to elaborate on that, if I may. Do you remember, was Judge Marinkovic the presiding judge?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: She was the presiding judge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know a Colonel Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you hear from him in any way before your evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. In fact, I was in contact with -- with General DZ and with Ciaglinski on the radio, and they are the ones that advised me that she had decided not to agree to go in with a light force but wanted to go in with a heavy force, and they basically told me to get the people out as quickly as possible. That's when I coordinated the evacuation of my verifiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On this report, I see these conditions the KLA was asking at the time. They asked MUP move back of hills; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it agreed with the judge or the Serb authorities in advance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What happened is we had been keeping in contact with the KLA in the villages and hoping that they would actually exercise restraint as well. We didn't want a huge fight to break out here and have all kinds of casualties on both sides, so we were -- we had been saying, you know, the presiding judge is going to come in with KVM, if we can manage to convince her to do so, so she can do an investigation, an independent investigation, and you know -- so we were trying to being very accommodating to both sides. But of course, tempers were very high, and the KLA did not want -- want this to happen. They didn't want any Serb presence in the village whatsoever. In spite of that, we continued to negotiate with them. And in fact it happened about the same time as she said, no, I'm going in with a heavy presence, that's when we received -- the KLA, okay, we'll agree, with these four conditions. So it was too late. It came after the fact, if you wish. So we weren't able to -- she hadn't agreed to them anyway, so it was too late and she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What concerns me is a matter of some principle. It's matter of sovereignty. A judge cannot enter the village without the protection of her own country. So that -- that seems to be the problem. What would be your assessment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's -- that's a good point. And in fact, we had no problem with having a -- having a light escort, i.e., if she had said I want to take one or two personal protection guards. But the MUP had deployed a complete company of MUP in armoured vehicles on the outsides -- on the outskirts of the village, and they wanted to go in and -- almost as another military operation. And that's what ended up happening; they went in with armoured vehicles and so forth, into the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it might be some useless question, but if the OSCE people had remained there and accompanied the investigating judge, had the KLA also fired the shootings against the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The KLA actually, you know, started retaliating but then moved out because they had a light presence, and in fact, the MUP began firing as opposed to going in and just escorting the judge. They mounted this as another military operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So even against the KVM people, if they had remained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they had remained there, yes. In fact, that was the concern of DZ, myself and all of the OSCE, was us getting caught in the middle of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I've been not too good with the exhibit numbers. Did we give page 8 an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. Exhibit 181.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And one question, if I might be at liberty. It's a question that I forgot to ask. Just my last question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, did you become aware of whether or not the Serb forces had suffered any casualties during the 15th of January 1999 incident?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I subsequently became aware that they had suffered one injury. There was one injury to one of their members.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And from a military perspective, what does the difference in casualties tell you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, if -- you know, 50 mostly civilians or -- I'll just say civilians on one side and one casualty only on the other side means that in fact the area would have seemed to be very lightly defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are my questions. Thank you very much, Major General, would you answer other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the rest of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Was it not entered as an exhibit under 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Meetings with the KLA commanders and some notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful to deal with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Certainly. I was simply following Your Honours' instruction that you wanted me to deal with those two particular areas, so I'm happy to deal with that now, if you want that live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pages 7 onwards, it may be helpful just to deal with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, if you could look at pages 7 and 6, which is the 17th of January notation of the record of discussions with the gentleman you've already referred to in evidence as Drini.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, this was meeting that I had in fact quite soon after -- on the 17th of January with KLA about -- about Racak. He seemed to be -- Commander Drini, at this point, was obviously very disappointed at the actions. He is the one that told me at this point that he had -- that the village had been very lightly defended, which was what our verifiers confirmed, and that the -- the attack there actually served to set a climate of fear amongst the people. In fact, this was corroborated later by our -- our people. After Racak happened, it -- on several occasions, we would get -- we received phone calls at 2.00 in the morning from villagers in some other village, villagers who were terrified because a MUP or unidentified white vehicle had driven through the city at 2.00 in the morning, and they -- the statement they always made was, "We don't want another Racak to happen." So Racak had actually set the scene for -- for great fear throughout -- throughout Kosovo. So this was a -- this was a meeting to discuss the arrangements there and what had happened and so forth. And what the -- to ensure that the response from the -- from the KLA was going to be muted and that they were going to continue to stick to the principles of the arrangement -- the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Turning next --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 182.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it Your Honours want me to deal with the remaining documents as well. I may as well just quickly go through those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The 28th of January 1999, page 5, appears to be a record of discussions again with Drini, held at the KLA meeting house.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. And this one here was about -- was after the events in Rogovo where about 25 Albanian people were killed, most of whom in this case certainly looked like they were KLA members. And I also wanted to discuss with -- with Drini at this point the opening of different field offices and what -- his actions in different areas. He, at one point, attempted to place a deadline on the KVM, and I in, I think about the fourth bullet from the bottom, I explained to him that the KVM did not do deadlines. This was more of a regular meeting with Drini.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your general impression of your meetings with Drini were what? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, again straightforward. He had been -- he had been a professional officer in the Yugoslav national army, the JNA, had done Staff College, in fact had gone to Staff College with the commander of 549 Brigade, Colonel Delic, which is one of the interesting situations you find yourselves in in some of these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 183.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Then there are some handwritten pages dated the 26th of February, 1999, and the 4th of March, 1999. One is called -- the 4th of March is called, "Points from Drini." Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No. That is Douglas Young, who is one of my verifiers. He's the one who actually had the meeting. I was not at this meeting. But this is a meeting when in fact he was -- Drini was actually taken to task for having targeted Serb villages, and that's at the point at which he mentioned that he knew the Geneva Conventions. And we were adamant that some of the problems that we were facing were because of -- of uncontrolled elements on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 184.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There's different handwriting for the 26th of February document.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. The 26th of February was a meeting at which my -- again my note-taker here was a Captain Weissflog. It was a meeting that took place after Randubrava, which was another incident where the KLA were attacked by the MUP there. Randubrava is a little village near Prizren, and this was more of a -- again a general meeting to discuss those events.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And finally, you don't appear to have been present at a meeting of the 23rd of January for Kostrice, but I take it these people were some of your verifiers, were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. Mike Morwood was the second in command of my -- of my Regional Centre, and the others were my verifiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the significance of this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Now, this one is on 23rd of -- 23rd of January, which was following another event where there was a car ambushed at Bela Crkva. We were discussing -- we were discussing the future and the -- again, this was another meeting where he was trying to put the 15-minute rule on us where if we didn't take action, KVM didn't take action within 15 minutes of an incident happening, that they were going to deal with it themselves, and that's when we told him that we don't do deadlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in these meetings, it's clear that the KVM was explaining to the KLA the terms and conditions that you were operating under; is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct. We were certainly -- we tried to -- to be impartial, and in my view we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Oh, last document number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will take the adjournment now. We'll start again at quarter past. General, would you remember in this and any other adjournment there may be in this case not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In cooperation with the Albanian terrorists, you were preparing the illegal criminal aggression of NATO against Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's preposterous. No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. So your answer is you did not; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: What was your question, that I was preparing NATO? No, I was not. And I was not in cooperation with anyone. I was an impartial international observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
