utterances.text: All right, we'll establish that. You started your statement by claiming the following in the first sentence: That you witnessed a crime. Since you have not been called here to judge whether something was a crime or atrocity or not, tell me, what are the official reports of the court authorities or the government authorities or of experts from Yugoslavia or elsewhere that you bore in mind when giving such an assessment of what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: My assessment is given in -- in light of my opinion and the events that I saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the task of the OSCE was to verify and monitor whether all the parties to the conflict were abiding by the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement. What were the conflict parties, and in your opinion, the terrorist organisation, the so-called KLA, could it have the -- could it be treated as a party to a conflict? This is on page 2, in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The parties that were in the agreement itself were the -- the Serb authority forces on one side and the KLA and Albanian locals on the other side. In terms of whether a conflict existed or not, this is a matter of legal -- matter which I'm not qualified to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, you wanted to make the KLA a legitimate legal force and, inter alia, you wanted to make it more accessible. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Accessible to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, more accessible in terms of cooperation, more open to cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The mission that I saw the OSCE as having was the verification of the agreement between yourself and Mr. Holbrooke, which had a number of -- which had a number of elements to it, one of which was to respect the ceasefire, to reduce levels of Serb forces, to -- to respect human rights and so forth. To do so, I did -- I had contact with the KLA, as they called themselves, and the Albanian local population, as well as the parties from the Serb authorities, both MUP, VJ, and administrative authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am saying the following: That you wanted to make the KLA a legitimate force and that, in that sense, you wanted to make them become more open to others. Therefore, I would like to recall a document presented by the other side. You are the author of that document. It's called "The Implementation of Measures for Implementing Contacts." The page of the Serbian version is 03036214. It says literally, if the KLA wants to be recognised as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. If you're going to put a document to the witness, he must see it so that he's able to respond to it. Has this document been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't believe it was, Your Honour. It may have -- my recollection doesn't serve me on this particular document, but my associate Mr. Higgins is checking as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can find it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what it says literally in the document: "However, if the KLA wants to be recognised as a legitimate force that is trusted, it has to be encouraged to become more accessible." So you're trying to present a terrorist organisation as a legitimate force. Please admit this as an exhibit. This is an OSCE document, and you're the author of this document. Here you are. I'm tendering it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find the document. Have you got the English of it there, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, no, but I just have the Serb translation, and it has a number from the other side and 03036214 -- 12 is what it says. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why were you dealing in this anyway? Why were you wondering what had to be done in order to make the KLA a legitimate force, a force that would be trustworthy, at that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I believe that the job of any international force, such as the KVM, has to develop trust with both parties or all parties to a conflict. In this case, I believe that the document you're referring to was a document that was looking towards measures that may be required in the event of an agreement between the Serb authorities and the -- the Albanian parties. And if that was the case, then we needed to put in place a certain regime of -- of not only verification but of shadow is what we had called it, where we would be accompanying the parties after an accord to ensure that both sides would comply with the accord. And so the whole question of trust, there's no doubt that when we dealt with both the Serb side and the Albanian side is that we acted on -- on a belief that trust would be developed between the parties, between the international community, which I represented as the OSCE, and the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I might interrupt just at the moment since Your Honours have asked. We have, we believe, located the statement, an English copy of that document, which is MM/6, can be brought to the courtroom in a moment or two. It was not exhibited, but I believe it is an attachment to his original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Why did you deal with this anyway? Why was it necessary for the KLA to be a legitimate force? I link this to the question that was put to you by Mr. Kwon in relation to sovereignty. Do you think that terrorist groups can, in any state, be treated as a legitimate party to a conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I can tell you the way I was trying to deal with both sides, and that includes the Serb authorities, by the way. I was trying to develop a level of trust where I could deal with them and actually request things from them and be told that things would -- certain things would happen so that we could verify their compliance with the agreement. And the agreement, again, was between yourself and Mr. Holbrooke, but included within the agreement was a certain behaviour by both your forces, the Serb authority forces, and the Albanian local forces, some of which were the KLA, self-proclaimed KLA, the local authorities -- Albanian local authorities, and the local population. And so we behaved totally -- we tried to behave totally impartially and verify the compliance of both sides to the agreement. It wasn't a matter of making anyone legitimate, but if we were going to deal with the Albanian side, we had to deal with them on the same basis of trust that we had with your forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we now have the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have one copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Copies can be brought down momentarily, but in fairness to the witness, perhaps he ought to see the document about which questions are being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness should see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. It is MM/2B, by the looks of things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's no good. The interpreters cannot hear you. Could you speak into the microphone. Now, has the -- rather than this, has the witness got the document MM/ --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got it. We in fact have it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was served with the original bundle, and it's MM/2B. I think this is it, 23rd of February, 1999? Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the one I have in front of me, Your Honour. In fact, it is the one that I mentioned which was a planning document which was never put into effect, but it was during the Rambouillet negotiations and we were leaning forward, if you wish, and planning for the eventual, hopefully, an agreement and looking at the measures that would be required in the event of such a -- an event. And as you see, that is -- in the introduction, that is what I say here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And while we're on it, is there any reference that you can remember to making them a legitimate organisation that the accused is asking you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you look at -- if you look at paragraph 4 -- the paragraphs are numbered. On page 2, paragraph 4 under KLA, it talks in there about the KLA's wish to be recognised as a credible and legitimate force, not that we wish to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quoted a sentence under paragraph 4A where you say: "However, if the KLA wishes to be recognised as a legitimate force that is believed, it has to be encouraged to become more accessible." That is the core of the matter, and I tender this into evidence, but we have to move on. I'm asking you whether you distinguish between --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I trust it will not matter. Let us exhibit the document the next Defence number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit D20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. General, if you'd like to hand that back into the Court if you would, please, and we can exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This takes up a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm giving documents that have already been registered, I mean that the other side already has. I really think that this much time should not be wasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get on with it, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because their authenticity is not questioned in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So do you distinguish between a political agreement between the government of the Republic of Serbia and the political representatives of the Kosovo Albanians and terrorists who kill, kidnap, and commit all sorts of other crimes on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, in this case, it was -- it was my duty on the ground to verify the agreement. The agreement called on both parties - your side, that is the Serb authorities in Kosovo, and the representatives of the Kosovo Albanians of all types - to comply with the provisions of the agreement, which were to in fact behave according to human rights. And the only way that -- one of which was to behave in accordance with human rights, to verify -- to comply with the ceasefire. And the only way that I could verify that and ensure that it did take place was to deal with all parties, on your side and on the Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us keep the questions and answers short, please. In your opinion, is the KLA a terrorist organisation or not? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: In my opinion, the KLA is an organisation that was -- that arose as a result of the -- the strife that the Albanian people were feeling on the ground. It was an assemblage of paramilitary forces, almost a rebel organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware of the assertion made by Robert Gelbard, the US envoy to the Balkans, that this is a terrorist organisation? I have already introduced this into evidence so I'm not going to tender it again. Are you aware of that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you must be aware of Security Council Resolution 1160 dated the 31st of March, 1998, and 1199 of the 23rd of September, 1998, then Resolution 1203 dated the 24th of October. All these Resolutions refer to terrorism in Kosovo. Isn't that correct? Therefore, why do you advocate having a terrorist organisation given legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not a fair question to the witness because it misrepresents what he said. He did not advocate legitimacy. He told you that he had to deal with both sides. Now, you've been told, Mr. Milosevic, before that we waste a lot of time by trying to reargue points which you assert and which the witness has answered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explain in your statement that KDOM practically became one with the Kosovo Verification Mission. This is page 3, paragraph 4. It practically melted into it. Those are your words. However, Drewienkiewicz, when he testified on the 11th of April, said that part of KDOM remained independent, to be precise, the US part of KDOM that remained in Kosovo throughout. He said literally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "We managed to absorb part of KDOM. However, that part of American KDOM which remained independent stayed on at Kosovo throughout." Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that this was a quotation from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who is right? Is it you or him? You say that KDOM melted into the Kosovo Verification Mission whereas he says that part of it remained independent. So who is right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: In terms of the -- the -- when the KVM was put in place, the KDOMs that already existed on the ground, most of the KDOMs were actually absorbed, and the -- the agreement in fact that you signed with Mr. Holbrooke actually talks about the OSCE was going to absorb the KDOMs that were already on the ground. In fact, this is what happened within my Regional Centre, is I -- I deployed and took under command the UK KDOM and portions of the US KDOM. But I also believe that the portions of the US KDOM remained outside the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You knew that then as well. Why is it that you managed only to absorb part of American KDOM and who stopped you from doing this? Or, rather, the question is: Did you lodge any kind of protest with the Security Council or anyone because it was impossible for you to place the American part of KDOM under the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: As I told you, I had a portion of the American KDOM under my command, under the KVM, and therefore, I was able, within my area, to operate with my forces without any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I assume that there is no contest, that according to the agreement, KDOM had to be absorbed into the Verification Mission, folded into it. I believe that that is not being challenged. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: In fact, some of the higher level agreements were not within my responsibility. I was given forces which included US KDOM, UK KDOM, portions thereof. I used them, and I -- in fact, I built up my forces on those portions of those two KDOMs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be inferred then -- can it be inferred then that members of American KDOM who were not folded into KVM Kosovo, that they actually acted contrary to the agreement? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: You would have to ask them that, because all the forces of the KDOM and the KVM that I saw acted in accordance with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you have any communication with American KDOM that was not under KVM control? Did you get any reports from them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were they deployed, the members of American KDOM who were not under your control like in Racak, Dragobil, Glodjane, all these places? You don't know? And in your opinion, why was there no agreement between you and the Albanians? I mean, let me clarify this question. When Drewienkiewicz testified on the 11th of April, he said: "We understood that one of the reasons why there was no agreement with the Kosovo Albanians who had hoped that this would be a tandem agreement to the agreement we signed in Belgrade in October was the fact that there was a public threat made that any Albanian who had any kind of agreement with Ambassador Hill or anybody from the international community would either be killed." So there was obviously no agreement with the Albanian side at any level, and I believe that that was one of the factors why there was no agreement of this nature. Do you agree with this assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the statement by General Drewienkiewicz or what you're talking about here, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So even if you don't know of this statement, did you know of the threats of the KLA, that they would kill any Albanian who would sign anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that threat, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know, from the period when you were in Kosovo, that certain Albanians who were loyal citizens of Serbia were killed by the KLA and were victims because they turned a deaf ear to these KLA threats. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you're not aware of that either, are you? You were head of the Regional Centre, as you explained. When you came, your first experience was that the Serb forces, as they are being called here, were cooperative all the time, and you had free access to local representatives. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what happened then? What changed this attitude? Was it the fact that you did not act in accordance with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: What happened to change what? I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was a change. You said first that the Serb forces were cooperative all the time and you had free access to local representatives. And you confirmed that that was right. Now, what happened? What changed this attitude? Was it the fact that you did not act in accordance with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The attitude of the Serb forces in my area was, for the most part, cooperative; i.e., when I wanted to have a meeting with the Serb representatives, I requested a meeting and for the most part I received acquiescence and managed to do so. After the Racak incident, the Urosevac brigade commander, however, did not behave in accordance with the way my, if I can call him that, my brigade commander - the brigade commander in my area - behaved. He refused to meet me or certainly did not meet me until three weeks later when I managed to get Colonel Kotur to convince him. So that was a change, and certainly wasn't because of a change in my behaviour or the behaviour of my verifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of the following: In the document that was provided by the other side, and you were the author of the document, it was disclosed along with your statement, it is called, "First Impressions, Prizren Regional Centre." On page number 03036013, that is the Serb version, and the English version 0075622, in the last paragraph, it says: "Throughout, the Serbian authorities were cooperative and we had free access to the local representatives." So I am going to tender this document of yours as well. I have it both in the English and Serbian languages. So please take a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to move on. I don't want to waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're putting things to a witness, he must have the chance of seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It's MM/2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: MM/2. We have that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which was the bit you were quoting to the witness, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the top of page 2, Your Honour, it says: "Throughout, the Serb authorities were cooperative and we had free access to local representatives." This is dated 23 December. It is, in fact, my first impressions after arriving about a week before, and I don't dispute that, that at that point, authorities were cooperative and I did have access when I requested it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement on page 7, in paragraph 1, you particularly highlighted the following, that Delic, that is the commander of the brigade who you talked to, he pointed out that Loncar was not his commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a commission of the federal government for cooperation with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That commission, including Loncar, could not have been in the chain of command, either of the army or of the police. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also, are you aware of the fact that Loncar actually became a member of that commission? He was the person who was there in Pristina and he was supposed to cooperate with the OSCE, and this was done at Walker's request in view of their former cooperation in Eastern Slavonia, that they knew each other and had a good cooperation. Oh, you're aware of that too, aren't you? And do you know that on the commission of the federal government, there was a total of 16 members and that Loncar was a retiree who, at Walker's request, was appointed to this team and that he was therefore in Pristina, otherwise, the chairman of the commission of the federal commission and that was appointed by the Federal Government was Nikola Sainovic, Deputy Prime Minister of the federal government. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of all the details that you've just given me but I was aware that Nikola Sainovic was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement, you deal with the contents of the talks between yourself and Delic, and as far as I was able to gather, he said on the occasion, "I'm just doing my job and preventing terrorists from infiltrating with weapons." He was guarding the border belt; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, this is also contained in the text which was disclosed by the Prosecution, which I should also like to tender into evidence. And you confirmed it, but I should like that document to be entered into the record. It is your own text: "I'm just doing my job and preventing terrorists from infiltrating with weapons. My personal opinion is that you can help us only in one way and that is to exert pressure on Albania so as to stop the shipment of arms across the border." And you say: "I agree. The Resolution of the Security Council ask that Albania stop bringing in weapons." I hope that that is not something that you're challenging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a document we have seen before and, yes, that's what Delic said and that's what I replied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this in the exhibit which we have? No need for it to be exhibited again, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He asked you to exert pressure on Albania to prevent this shipment of arms, and you agreed to do that; right? And I quoted this a moment ago because it was contained in the UN Security Council Resolution which demanded that Albania cease this practice; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I agreed that I had to pressure the Albanian side but I could not, obviously, pressure the country of Albania. But every meeting I had with the KLA or with local representatives, I -- I admonished them to ensure that they would not bring -- bring weapons and smuggle arms across the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your area, there was heavy fighting between the terrorists and the regular forces of the Yugoslav army and police force; is that correct? And in fact, you say that on page 3 in the last paragraph of your statement. You say: "There was fierce fighting between the terrorists and the regular forces of the army and the police"; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: There had been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This region, this area which came under your authority was one of the strongholds of the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't think -- it would depend how you would signify or define a stronghold. Certainly there was a strong KLA presence in my area, as there was in other areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is the observation correct that the Kosovo border region was and remains the smuggling route for drugs, arms, humans, and that only with the abolishment of the KLA could the border be secured? Would that observation be correct, to your mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Definitely the border area was an area where there was a lot of smuggling across the border. Whether the abolishment of the KLA would be a way to stop it, I can't say whether that would work or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says in the OSCE document which has also been registered by the opposite side. It is your statement too. It says: "For several centuries, the Kosovo border region was used as an important route of contraband and smuggling for drugs, arms, human beings, livestock, et cetera --" I apologise to the interpreters for reading out so fast. "-- and of late, weapons and members of the KLA too." Now, "If the KLA were to be abolished completely, this lack of law and order in Albania and Albanian border patrols will make the authorities in Kosovo secure their borders." That was also something that the OSCE mission wrote, and I'd like to tender that into evidence as well, that particular document. Now, I'm sure you're acquainted with the fact that the KLA was procuring weapons and rockets as well. You were told that personally; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Personally by whom? I had heard rumours that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just rumours? They didn't tell you personally?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Who would tell me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, in the document of the other side, whose author you are, which was disclosed with your witness statement, on the minutes of the 17th -- the meeting of the 17th of January, 1999, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down in quoting figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The English version is K0075715, it says that the regional commander of the KLA, Drini, told you that he needed to get supplies of arms with special range firing abilities and rockets of the Katyusha type. So these weren't rumours. He told you that specifically although you don't remember him saying so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... General, can you deal with that or would you like to see the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have it here, Your Honour, if you'd like to give me a second. Is there a date to that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 17th of January. I understand it to be the meeting with Drini. Don't interrupt. The meeting with Drini. It's our Exhibit 182, for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting this. "D" is Drini, and it says: "D" Drini, Regional Commander, "M" Brigadier General Maisonneuve, and "C" is Chris Cobb-Smith, the liaison officer, et cetera, et cetera. The rest isn't important. "D: In the context of talks as to the exposure to special fire, he spoke about the need to procure special range weapons possibly of the Katyusha type."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: So he did say that, I guess, at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have this here. I have the English. "In the context of receiving indirect fire, he spoke of the need to acquire indirect fire weapons, maybe Katyusha rockets." That is what is contained in your own report. So it is not a question of rumours, it is information that you received at the meeting with the commander whom you call Drini. And a moment ago, you mentioned him and said that you had regular meetings with him. You used the term "regular," I believe, regular meetings. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what are you, as the KVM -- what did you do to prevent activities of this kind which were obviously, as we noted a moment ago, were contrary to the UN Security Council Resolution to the tasks that you had? So what did you undertake to prevent activities of this kind?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, actually, what we undertook was to ensure that, first of all, we would mention it at meetings that we had with -- with both sides, with -- particularly with the Albanian side. And as well, we patrolled as much as possible the areas around the border. Now, the problem we had, of course, was that the Serb forces would not allow us to get close to the border and to have freedom of movement, as the agreement had said, in the area. So we were partly kept from doing our job by the Serb side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is in contradiction with what you observed a moment ago, that they didn't prevent you but were cooperative. Did they prevent you or did they not prevent you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I said they were cooperative in our dealings, I did not say that they were cooperative in allowing us freedom of movement in all the areas that we were supposed to have. But when they did request -- when I requested a meeting, I did usually get acquiescence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you knew full well there were KLA plans to revive hostilities in January 1999 and that the following steps taken by the KLA was to transfer the campaign into the towns. They informed you of that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If it isn't, then let me remind you that in the document whose author you are, which was disclosed along with your statement, on page 03035957 Serbian version, points 4 and 8, and K00570.4 and 7, it says: "Plans to revive hostilities are completed. The transference of the campaign to the towns is an active element of the forthcoming steps to be taken by the KLA," or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you in just a moment. It is the minutes from the meeting with the KLA on the 23rd of January, Kostrice, 1500 hours, Morwood, Cobb-Smith, Lefever, Drini - one, two, three, four from the top - "Plans of the KLA for hostilities on a broad scale have been completed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's -- let us -- Mr. Milosevic, let us find the document. It's Exhibit 186.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I have the document here, Your Honour. In fact. It was -- it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a meeting at which I was not -- this was done by the four people that are there, the three from the KVM and the one from the KLA. I did see the document after, in fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was something you knew about. You said a moment ago that you didn't know about it. And at the beginning, you say that you're giving information not only on the basis of your own personal impressions but also on the basis of the reports sent in by your verifiers, which is quite logical because if all that was needed were your own personal impressions, I don't think you would need 1.300 verifiers. And it says here in the original document, your document K0075720: [In English] "KLA plans for a more general resumption of hostilities were complete." And at the bottom, it says: [In English] "Taking the campaign to the towns was an active element in the 'next military steps' of the KLA."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. As I said, I did see it, I guess, at the time. In fact, that's my signature at the bottom that I say that I'd seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as a KVM -- as the KVM, what did you do to prevent this development of events? These are serious things, to transfer terrorism to the towns, to revive hostilities, et cetera, et cetera. What did you undertake, as the KVM, to prevent all this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, we -- we had a very aggressive patrol scheme, an aggressive scheme of liaison with the parties to ensure that they would not take any kind of action such as that. That's the -- in fact, that was the problem with the KVM was the matter of how do you impose a solution? We could not impose a solution; we could not force the parties, either the Serb side or the Albanian side, to comply. We had to actually speak to them, to liaise with them and to make them understand that their behaviour should be a certain way. In the case of the Albanian side, we often received threats and admonishment and they would tell us that they were going to take some action, and we continued to -- to explain to them that we weren't going to reply to threats. We were not going to use threats and agree to do -- behave a certain way. With either side. We didn't agree to any threats, and we would refuse to be threatened. So this was not the first time they talked to us about hostilities and so on. This was barely a week after Racak, so they were very -- they were very tense still and -- and we were trying to get them to relax and not to retaliate after the Racak operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider, Mr. Maisonneuve, that at that point, in view of the seriousness of this type of information that you received, that a public condemnation and publication of threats of this kind would have been fruitful in order to suppress activities of this kind? Public condemnation by the KVM and making these threats public, would that have been fruitful in suppressing these activities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The KVM received all meeting records. We sent them up to them as -- as documentation. Then it was up to the KVM to actually take action. Let me tell you, though, that whenever the KLA actually carried out such actions, we did come forward and denounce them. And a particular example is the three policemen that were killed in the pass on the 8th of January. We put out a press release and we were very forward in denouncing these actions by the KLA, just as we were very forward in denouncing the actions of the Serb -- Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As for the killed policemen, I understand that, but I'm asking you this: These threats that were very serious and which you received officially, at an official meeting where minutes were kept, were they not reasons to condemn this and to make them public, to publish them in order to suppress these activities? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: In terms of making things public, this was not within my domain. I did not have the authority to make anything public. I would send them up to the KVM headquarters and they would decide what was public and what was not. And we received threats like this all the time, from both sides, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that came under Walker's competence, did it, not your own?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say you arrived in December 1998, that you arrived in Pristina, and that you mentioned that 35 people were killed who were members of the KLA, and this was a legitimate military operation; isn't that right? That's what it says on page 4, paragraph 2 of your statement. You say that: "In all respects, it was a legitimate military operation." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That was my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now in your statement, on page 11, paragraph 3, you say that, in your area, there were acts on the part of the KLA which could be assessed as war crimes and from that it emerges that you were informed with the activities being taken by the KLA. According to your knowledge or the knowledge gained by your colleagues, the KLA in March, 1998, was already preparing for war, and according to your information, the KLA recruited people for war already at that time. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't know what document you're referring to in this case here. I don't think I made any assessment of what was going on in March of 1998. I was not on the ground at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm thinking of your -- of your overall knowledge and information as to the preparations for war, recruitments being carried out and especially for this assessment and evaluation. And you're asking about the document. It is page 11, paragraph 3 of your statement, where you say that the conduct of the KLA could be characterised as a war crime -- war crimes. "I am aware of behaviour by the KLA that could be assessed as war crimes."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. I did in fact have in, I believe, the end of February of 1999, the KLA actually took two Serb civilians hostage, and I spent a long, long time negotiating with the KLA and speaking to them to let them -- to let them go, and I -- in fact, I spent a long time with the Serb authorities, explaining what was going on and taking care of ensuring that both sides were aware of what was going on. Because of our results, the KVM intervention, in fact, they did -- the KLA did manage to release one of the prisoners alive and the other had been killed and beaten. And those were observations that we made at the time. So I believe that is also against, obviously, human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since in your statement on page 11, paragraph 3, you say that the heads of the coordinating centres liaised directly with other KLA representatives, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted), on page 1 -- the number is 03036808. That witness was for the Nerodime area. And he says that in March 1998, following orders from the main headquarters of the KLA, they left and went to other parts to recruit people for war. And that is to be found in his statement. Are you aware of that? Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, many of the KVM link this to a year of change. Is it true that these changes were precisely the consequence of the activities of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The great -- major changes that took place in the sense of the expansion of the KLA in 1998, the KLA expanded in 1998, is it true that these changes are precisely the result of the activities of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, the KVM deployed as of October, November, December of 1998, so that's very much towards the end, and I don't know how the -- it could have influenced any KLA expansion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about, that end-of-year period. Up until the arrival of the KVM, you see, they were completely thwarted. Now, to clarify this question, Ramush Haradinaj, for instance, one of their heads, the heads of these KLA criminals whose activities are well-known to the other side too, in a book, "Stories of War and Freedom, Talks with Ramush Haradinaj," on page 116 and 117, says that the arrival of the verifiers, the OSCE verifiers to Kosovo enabled the revival of the KLA, and the meetings with the verifiers were very long, lengthy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to be helped by this. I don't know what you're talking about. Some book, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a book. I have the introduction and the beginning. Achieved agreement by Holbrooke, save the KLA, et cetera. The Verification Mission. I haven't got the entire book, but I will be providing a copy in English for you but I'd like to tender this into evidence because this document speaks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we're not going to have it tendered into evidence. It's just a book and somebody's opinion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not somebody's opinion. It is testimony by somebody who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not testimony. Testimony is evidence which is given from the stand over there in this case. It's nothing else. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, even the witness of the Prosecution, for which you did not want to have the name mentioned a moment ago, explains in his statement that in 1998, upon the arrival of the KVM, changes took place and that the political goal was left behind because of the negative reaction on the international plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't answer questions like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you explain in your statement on page 5, last paragraph, that the Verification Mission could verify the violations of the agreement throughout Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you verify the fact that the KLA was burgeoning when the order came to mobilise the population, that is to say men over the age of 18 to be mobilised? Did you verify this fact, this information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you happen to know that it was precisely this order to mobilise which was issued, that it was issued very close to the illegal NATO aggression against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have an opinion as to why that order went hand-in-hand with the beginning of the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Irrelevant? All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, during your sojourn, did you verify, for example, in your area of responsibility the -- how many KLA members were armed, were under arms?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Verified, you mean in terms of counting and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your assessments. Did you verify the -- how many KLA members there were in view of the meetings you had, the information that was coming in from them, the general picture that you were able to gain sounding out the terrain? Do you know how many of them there were in the area, their units, the composition of their units, the weapons they had, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: We didn't have specific numbers and weren't able to gather specific numbers of totals and so forth. We had a general idea of how many KLA and where they were and how they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The OSCE monitored the events in Racak on the 15th of January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this event was followed from the very morning, was monitored from the early morning; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Early morning on the 15th. No, actually it was monitored once we heard there was -- there was an attack going in. And the verifiers, I can't say exactly what time the verifiers got there on the 15th itself, but they were there midday, I would say, probably, and were there until the evening on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 9, in the one but last paragraph, you say that they monitored these actions from a hill above Racak and that the verifiers saw smoke coming out of the chimneys in the village, which told them that the civilian population was going about their usual daily morning duties.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in your statement. Now, if, according to what they observed, they were going about their normal daily village duties, then it was morning, right, when they turned up, when they came? Is that the logical conclusion which can be drawn and which can be deduced from your own statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I guess that would mean they can't go about their duty for the rest of the day if they do it only in the morning, according to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that, and I was quoting from what you said, that this indicated that the population was going about their daily morning duties. Now, if you took note of that, that they were going about their normal daily duties, it means that you were there from the morning. You weren't able to observe daily morning duties in the afternoon, for example. And as you yourself state on page 8, paragraph 2, you went to Racak on the 15th. Now, what was your report on what you were able to ascertain on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: On the 15th, as has been already discussed in one of my reports, I arrived in the area about 1630, myself, 1630, 1700 hours. My verifiers had been on the ground before, and as mentioned before, they -- they had seen the action, part of the action that was going on in Racak. When I arrived, I went to the hospital and arranged for medical help for the wounded people, and -- so that -- I arrived on the ground, as I say, about 1600, 1700.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you arrived there. Your verifiers were there from the morning, they were observing what was going on. Then you came in after your verifiers, about 4.00 p.m., and you established what the situation was. What did you write in that report when you got there? You were in Racak on the 15th. So what did you find there? What did you establish there, rather?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: What I established was that there had been an action within Racak, that we had seen tanks and armoured personnel carriers taking part in the action, the VJ on the high ground firing towards occupied houses, and that we had seen the MUP go into the village and clear the village house to house. At that point, we also established that -- my verifiers established that there had been some wounded people, and we brought them out of the village the evening of the 15th, and that's what I reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But just awhile ago, this morning when you were speaking, you said -- I'm paraphrasing what you said, but it is in the transcript, that the verifiers said to you that there was shooting on the outskirts of the village, around the village, not at the houses -- not at the houses in the village. So the word you used was "the outskirts" of Racak, and that's what your verifiers said to you. That's what you said only awhile ago. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes. In Racak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you came in on the 15th of January, were there any members of the KLA in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm told that there were. I received reports from my verifiers that they were lightly -- light -- lightly held at that point. A few members, and I can't say how many exactly, but there were a few members of the KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So already in the afternoon when you arrived, the village was under KLA control yet again. You do know, I hope, that the entire world public has been informed by your boss, the head of KVM, Walker, that there was a massacre in Racak, that civilians were killed, and that a reaction followed from all quarters. Mr. Nice actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's very difficult to follow if you're not asking questions. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if that kind of assessment was made, although an on-site investigation had not been carried out and the results of the post-mortems had not come in, why was such an assessment given without the data that you obtained or that you could have obtained from the KLA and its commanders?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a question that I can't answer because it was done by -- by Ambassador Walker. That was his assessment. Is that what you're asking me, whether -- why was the assessment done?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Maisonneuve, in view of your obligations as a verifier - and I assume that there is also your obligation to tell the truth - you had to know, on the 15th when you entered Racak that it was KLA members who were killed there. Isn't that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: On the 15th, I did not know that KLA members had been killed. In fact, I did not know that civilians had been killed either. It was on the 16th that we discovered the bodies, and I can tell you, from my observations, that these bodies were civilians. In my assessment, they were not members of the KLA, the bodies that we found. An 18-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy are not members of the KLA, to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not asking you about the boy. I'm asking you about whether you knew that KLA members had been killed. And since your answer is no, I would like to remind you of the following: That in a document that you authored and that was provided by the Prosecution which is called "Report of the Regional Centre," 03035952 is the number of the Serbian version, the last paragraph, it says Assessment. The English version is 030 -- 0075712. The last paragraph says: "A number of members of the KLA were killed and a few were wounded." That's what it says here in your document.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: This assessment was written on the 16th of January, Mr. Milosevic, not on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume, since the 16th comes after the 15th, that you did write on the 16th what you established on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are not -- you are not being just to the witness. He's told you clearly that on the 15th, he didn't know, but by the 16th, he did. Now, are we going to advance any more by this particular line of argument? I think not. Can we move on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is not being challenged at all, because I asked him whether members of the KLA were killed and whether he had to know about that, and he said no. And in his report of the 16th of January, it says that members of the KLA were killed. You can see this on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he didn't know on the -- just -- just -- you haven't been paying attention. He said he didn't know on the 15th. That was his point. Then on the 16th, he's included it in his report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the 16th, as far as I know, Walker proclaimed that this was a massacre of civilians. The 16th, not the 15th. So it was on this day, the 16th, when Walker proclaimed that there was a massacre of civilians in the report that bears the date of the 15th of January. And then on the 16th of January, that is to say that this was said on the 16th, it says that KLA members were killed. That is to say on the day when Walker speaks of a massacre of civilians in the official OSCE report, it says it is KLA members who were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All it says is a number of KLA members were killed. Now, what is the point of all this examination? I think we're just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point, Mr. May, is very simple, and it pertains to the difference between a massacre of civilians and loss of lives by members of the KLA, and I consider that to be quite different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you putting? Are you putting to this witness -- so that we can understand, are you putting to the witness that the dead bodies he saw were members of the KLA? Is that the point that you're putting to him? Because if that's the suggestion, he should have the opportunity of answering it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that what it says in the OSCE report, that the OSCE knew on the 16th, that is to say on the day when Walker proclaimed that a massacre of civilians had taken place, that Walker knew this because he put it in his report in writing that it was members of the KLA who were killed. That is what I claim. And what the witness saw, I cannot claim anything of that nature, what the witness saw with his very own eyes. But that he did know on the 16th of January that KLA members were killed and that is the day that Walker talked about a massacre of civilians, that is something I do know and I imagine that is not being contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General Maisonneuve, have you understood any of that, and can you comment on it if you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess I can say that my assessment on the evening of the 16th, which is the portion that he's referring to in the actual assessment, is that I thought at that point that a number of KLA members were killed in the village; but on top of that, of course, what came out was a whole number of civilians, definitely more than eight or -- certainly there were at least 20 and I believe I do mention in there up to about 50 is how many we thought had been killed in the village at that time, most of whom were civilians. I -- when I looked at the bodies myself on that day, all the bodies that I saw, I could not say that they would have been members of the KLA. They were people of older -- elderly people. Most looked like farmers, or very young as the boy and young lady were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it is of assistance, I believe it's Exhibit 180 to which reference has been made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were in contact with the KLA that day in the afternoon, and this is what a Prosecution witness says -- I'm not going to mention his name: "The commander of the Operative Zone --" I'm going to skip some portions in order to save time, everything that he describes, how things started on the morning of the 15th of January between 6.00 and 7.00, that they did expect an attack and that they had fortified themselves -- "that the Serb forces approached our positions so shooting started. In the bunker, we had two soldiers who had fired three bullets which caused the soldiers in Racak to be on the alert. That was the signal." Then in his statement, the commander of the zone, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot help about what this particular witness said. I'm going to stop this examination. It's quite pointless putting to this witness. You can put it to that one. There's no point putting it to this one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I want to present these facts, and I want to link this up with the fact that the witness, General Maisonneuve, was in contact with the KLA and that they did inform him of these facts. I would like him to give me an answer. Did they inform them about any of these facts? I think that my question is quite legitimate. Since your witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, stop reading. When you met the KLA, General, did they tell you about any assault or any defence of Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. He says in his statement: "Nine soldiers killed during the first attack." I'm not going to mention their names although he does mention all the names. And then he says, further on, that: "In Racak, from October, November 1998, there were 47 soldiers of the KLA who were staying in the house owned by Muhamet Mustafa, who was one of the killed persons. They were called the unit of Racak. They had certain places where they took up positions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're wasting time. You are trying to make speeches. The Prosecution case, and you should understand it, is this: That there may have been some fire from the KLA but that what happened was that people were killed and executed and the bodies found, and those are the bodies which the witness saw. They were not, they say, members of the KLA. Now, no doubt it will be an issue for us to determine whether they were or not, and we will, but we are not assisted by constant repetition of evidence about which the witness cannot help us. You can call your own evidence in due course. I have in mind that this witness has important public duties to perform, and he's being kept here, and the time of the Court is being taken up by this effort on your part to simply have your side read out continuously. Now, have you got any other questions you want to ask the witness? Have you any other questions you want to ask this witness rather than argue with him about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I protest categorically because, yesterday, Mr. Nice was spending as much time as he wanted yesterday here, and he said that Racak was a turning point in the events in Kosovo. You are not allowing me to legitimately cross-examine about that, and you assert that that is irrelevant. I think that this is the gravest and most serious violation of my rights until now in terms of presenting the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have not said that this is irrelevant. It's very important. What is irrelevant and improper is the way that you continue with cross-examination, reading out lengthy statements, frequently not asking questions about them, and dealing with matters which the witness can't help about. You have been told before that you will have the opportunity to call your own evidence. What you're supposed to do is to ask the witness about matters that he can deal with rather than reading out chunks of statements to him. Now, there is quarter of an hour left. If you want to cross-examine this witness about something else, you should do so now rather than continuing in this particular line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying that I do not have the right to cross-examine him for more than 15 minutes more? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider it. But if you waste time with constant argument, then we're very unlikely to grant you more time. Now, I suggest you move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not additional time at all, Mr. May. You are making it impossible for me to cross-examine, and it's not the first time. And especially now with this kind of key issue as Racak is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Maisonneuve, your verifiers who were observing, did they inform you about this? Because this stems from the report of the zone commander that around 11.30 -- after 11.30, a counter-offensive started, that from Petrovo, they attacked Serbs in Racak with mortars and mortars hit the targets. That is after all the heavy weapons that Mr. Drewienkiewicz recognised when he was watching the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is exactly the point that I've been making; a constant speech from you. Now, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did your verifiers inform you about the counter-attack carried out by the KLA? And it seems obvious here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The answer is no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On that day, you did have contact with the KLA. And you could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which day did he have contact with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he confirmed that he had contacts with the KLA on the 15th. So could you establish what their activities were, and could you not inform the world public of that side of the matter as well that I have been receiving to and the matter about which the commander of their zone gave a statement as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, on the 15th of January, my observers, my verifiers, had contact with the KLA and confirmed to me that, in their view, the KLA had a very small presence in the village. And in my meetings subsequent to the 15th, this is what they also confirmed to me, the KLA did, that they had held the village very lightly and had not put up resistance in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of soldiers they were is not a matter for you to testify about and I'm not asking you about that, and everybody knows about that, for that matter. They fled like rabbits and they only shot from ambushes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is exactly what I'm going to say, and I shall now -- I shall now consider whether we should continue this cross-examination. Just a moment. I'm going to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will allow this cross-examination to continue, Mr. Milosevic, but on this basis: That you ask short questions. Throughout this trial you've been making speeches instead of asking questions. The Trial Chamber has in mind that you're acting in person and you're not a professional advocate and, therefore, some leeway has to be given. But it's now time to stop the speech-making and begin concentrating on questions. You've had enough time to learn. You're not entirely new at it. So you have that warning, and unless there are questions from now on, cross-examination will be stopped. General, can you come back sometime between now and -- we will go on for another ten minutes. Can you come back to allow further cross-examination sometime between now and July the 26th? Can you make yourself available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on that day, that is to say on the 15th of January, around 17.15 hours, the OSCE contacted Fehmi Muja, an officer in charge of moral and political questions in the KLA? Otherwise, he wore civilian clothes. He did not carry weapons. Is it correct that they contacted him and that, through him, a meeting was scheduled with the commander of the zone and then that meeting was held in Petrovo on that day -- that evening, rather? Is that correct? At that meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just stop there. Stop there. The first question is: Was there a meeting? Let the witness deal with it and then you can go on asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Walker meet with any KLA commanders on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: On the 16th, I believe he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know -- or, rather, were you with Walker in Racak on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I was in Racak, but I was not at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the meeting held in Petrovo at 1300 hours?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the exact times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Walker tell you that he was then informed about the entire military situation and about what had been happening, that he was informed by the Zone Commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the witness I spoke about personally showed to the investigator of the Tribunal all the positions that they operated against Racak then, the KLA, that is, and within Racak, too, and where 47 soldiers were positioned and where the headquarters was and the positions in Racak and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have been told to keep the questions short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was not aware that this person had shown the positions, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many bodies were buried at the cemetery in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: You mean when they buried the bodies that were killed at Racak?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. How many bodies after that? Of course, I'm not talking about the cemetery from its very inception, no. Then.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I believe it must be around 40 to 45. There was a long period where the bodies were sent to Pristina before they were handed over to -- they were handed over back to the Albanian community there, and I don't know exactly how many were buried on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very often there are these two different figures that one comes across, the ones that you mentioned a short while ago, Mr. Maisonneuve. How many persons were killed in Racak; 40 or 45?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't have the exact numbers in my head, but I'm led to believe it was 45. The human rights verifiers that came from Pristina on the 16th and thereafter were the ones that were actually looking after and determining exactly how many bodies were found. I know my verifiers throughout the day of the 16th were finding bodies as they went along and looked at -- did their patrol within the village and talked to the Albanian side. Certainly, as I was driving there myself on the morning of the 16th, I was hearing reports and bodies -- the body count was going 20, 25, and so forth. By the time -- by the time that the 16th ended, I believe the body count was about between 40 and 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about these five that keep missing? Who are these five who are never there? You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that at the funeral, because the KVM was present, a number of Albanians were arrested. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't know, because my people -- my verifiers were not there. Racak is outside of my area and the -- the burial took place in Regional Centre 5's area. So I did not have any of my verifiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you were explaining this today, that because a head of the Regional Centre was not appointed, Regional Centre number 5, that this is what you were entrusted with as a prominent member of the mission, a general, et cetera? That is what I seem to understand from the explanation you gave this morning, that you were appointed.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right, the actual operation during the Racak time, so the 15th, 16th, 17th. And then the operation was handed over back to the deputy head which actually did exist for Regional Centre 5. They were operating with a deputy head in the Regional Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of what you've just said, that means that all reports that any verifiers would obtain in any context for the dates of the 15th, 16th, and 17th that you just mentioned, would have had to reach you as well. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The verifiers that belonged to Regional Centre 5 would operate with me on the ground. We would gather their information obviously as much as we could, but then they would go back to their regional centre at the end of the day and make their normal reports up their normal chain of command with the deputy commander of Regional Centre 5 and up to the KVM. It's a matter of how the information is fused. So, in this case, my verifiers reported through me, obviously, to the KVM headquarters and the Regional Centre 5 verifiers reported through their own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must -- we must adjourn. It's quarter to two. General, would you please arrange to come back for that -- speak to the Prosecution about that, of course, to make the arrangements. If you would come back, we would be grateful, before the 26th of July. We shall allow cross-examination of another hour and a half when the witness returns. Thank you. We will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
